title: Ten to one in a buffer
hook: Ten times more acid than base. Where does the pH land?

knows: that a buffer holds a stock of a weak acid and its base (one-dose-of-acid)
that pH is a log scale (ph-log-scale)
doesNotKnow: that a buffer's pH is set by the log of the base-to-acid ratio, not by the amounts

misconception: More buffer, or more of the acid, changes the pH in proportion.
objective: The learner can explain that pH = pKa + log10(base/acid), so an acetate buffer with 10 times as much acid as base has pH about 3.76, one unit below pKa 4.76, and that equal amounts give pH = pKa however much buffer there is.

claims.text: Acetic acid has a pKa of about 4.76 at 25 °C.
claims.source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 'Dissociation constants of organic acids in aqueous solution': acetic acid pKa 4.756 at 25 °C.

claims.text: A buffer's pH is pKa + log10(base ÷ acid) (Henderson-Hasselbalch), so 10 times as much acid as base gives about 4.76 − 1 = 3.76.
claims.source: Henderson-Hasselbalch equation (Atkins & Jones, Chemical Principles, ch. on buffers; Harris, Quantitative Chemical Analysis, ch. 9). 4.76 + log10(10/100) = 3.76 (node; Demo.tsx pH()).

claims.text: Each tenfold change in the base-to-acid ratio moves the pH by 1; equal amounts give pH = pKa however much buffer there is (on stage, after 100 acid : 10 base, the learner sets equal amounts other than 10 of each, e.g. 100 of each, and the marker sits back at 4.76).
claims.source: From c2: log10(10) = 1; log10(1) = 0 for any equal amounts (10:10, 100:100, 1:1 all give 4.76 on the stage). Demo.tsx v3: milestone scaled-equal requires equal amounts different from the start after the 10:1 state; the reveal quotes the amount the learner set. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Own node: pH(b, a) = 4.76 + log10(b/a); 10:10, 100:100, 1:1, 3:3, 30:30 all give 4.76; 100:10 gives 3.76; ratio x10 changes pH by exactly 1. Demo v3 milestone 'scaled-equal' fires only for equal amounts other than 10 after the 100:10 state; reveal quotes that amount.

claims.text: More buffer only makes the pH harder to push (more buffer capacity).
claims.source: Buffer capacity grows with the total buffer concentration (Harris, Quantitative Chemical Analysis, ch. 9, 'buffer capacity'; one-dose-of-acid lesson). | WITHDRAWN v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): sentence removed from the reveal; nothing on stage showed it (r5 finding).

claims.text: The equation holds well for moderate concentrations, about 0.01 to 1 mol/L.
claims.source: Henderson-Hasselbalch neglects water's own ions and activity coefficients; it fails for very dilute buffers or ratios far from 1 (Harris, ch. 9; Po & Senozan, J. Chem. Educ. 78, 1499, 2001). Range quoted as a rule of thumb; the stage's amounts (mmol) are assumed to be in a volume giving such concentrations. · Fact-check 2026-10-13: Po & Senozan, J. Chem. Educ. 78:1499 exists but the 0.01-1 M range could not be read in it. Independent check: exact concentration-only calc for acetic acid 10:1 differs from the equation by 0.01 pH at 1 M, 0.07 at 0.01 M, 0.32 at 0.001 M; activity effects at 1 M are not computed. Rule of thumb is fair.

claims.text: A buffer is a mixture of a weak acid (HA) and its partner base (A−) that resists changes in pH; its pKa is the pH it sits at when the two are present in equal amounts.
claims.source: Standard general-chemistry definitions (IUPAC Gold Book: buffer solution; acid dissociation constant). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 19): Derivation: Ka = [H+][A-]/[HA], so [A-] = [HA] gives [H+] = Ka, pH = pKa (Henderson-Hasselbalch, which the stage uses). Buffer capacity beta = 2.303 C Ka[H+]/(Ka + [H+])^2 is largest at pH = pKa, so the mixture resists pH change. Matches the IUPAC definition of a buffer solution (I could not open the Gold Book; host blocked). Stage question uses the same wording.

recall.question: A buffer with pKa 7.2 holds 10 times as much base as acid. Its pH is about…
recall.why: pH = pKa + log10(base/acid) = 7.2 + log10(10) = 8.2. A tenfold ratio moves pH by one unit.
